newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch call rates collapse ahead of credit expiry.
newsitem.headline: Dutch call rates collapse ahead of credit expiry.

text.p: Overnight guilder rates collapsed on Monday in a market awash with liquidity ahead of Friday's expiry of the three-month secured loans quota.

With bid rates for call money down more than a full percentage point from last Friday's 3.18 percent, activity was concentrated on one-day money and longer-dated guilders remained virtually untouched.

Call had opened at 3.06 percent bid but fell sharply almost immediately, dealers said. At around 1200 GMT overnight guilders were quoted at between 2.0-2.25 percent bid/offer, with one dealer reporting trades at two percent.
"We had expected some pressure on call money rates, but we hadn't planned on them falling quite this far," one dealer said.
The three-month secured loans quota allows commercial banks to borrow from the Dutch central bank at the lowest official rate, which is currently pegged at 2.50 percent.
Commercial banks tend to build up "savings" during the three months the quota has to run, utilizing them in the final days as a source of cheap money.
As a result call money prices tend to fall immediately ahead of an expiry as major players shun the open market.
The phenomenon was exaggerated this time around partly because some banks took in additional liquidity last week, fearing they had eaten too much into their credit quotas.
Consequently they were well-covered on Monday. The treasury, also an active seeker of liquidity last week, was similarly holding back as Treasury Certificate (DTC) proceeds came in.
Dealers said demand for call was limited. "That's why bid rates are going down and down," one said.
The guilder was bid at 112.4225 per 100 marks, a touch firmer than Friday's 112.425 fixing.
